title: Everyday Serbo-Croatian: beginner practice
description: Original beginner teaching material. This is a self-check, not an official examination or a CEFR certification. The material awaits native-speaker review.
language_notes: The examples prioritize Serbian and Montenegrin usage. Serbian also has Ijekavian speakers, and forms cross borders. Variants are examples, not exclusive national labels. Ordinary spelling does not consistently show stress.

lessons.title: Meet someone
lessons.body: Use Dobar dan as a polite daytime greeting. Zovem se introduces your name, and Drago mi je means pleased to meet you. Kako si? is familiar singular; Kako ste? addresses someone politely or more than one person.

examples.english: Good day! My name is Ana.

lessons.title: Read both scripts
lessons.body: Serbian and Montenegrin can be written in Latin or Cyrillic. The Latin digraphs lj, nj and dž each correspond to one Cyrillic letter: љ, њ and џ. Latin j sounds like English y in yes; č and ć are different sounds. Montenegrin also has ś and ź, with Cyrillic с́ and з́; their use varies. A transliteration changes script, not the regional word or pronunciation.

examples.note: An example of the letter nj; the word changes form with grammar.

lessons.title: Notice useful variants
lessons.body: Ekavian mleko and Ijekavian mlijeko both mean milk; gde and gdje both mean where. Ijekavian is common in Montenegro, while both Ekavian and Ijekavian are used by Serbian speakers. Sjutra and sutra both occur in Montenegro. Croatian often uses kruh for bread; hljeb and hleb are also regional words for bread. Kava is common in Croatian; kafa and kahva also occur, including in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

examples.note: Both forms are used in Montenegro.

lessons.title: Say who you are
lessons.body: Short forms of biti, to be, include ja sam, ti si and on or ona je. Imam means I have. The subject pronoun can often be omitted when the verb ending makes the person clear.

lessons.title: Describe how you feel
lessons.body: Some adjectives change according to the speaker. A man can say Gladan sam; a woman can say Gladna sam. These are masculine and feminine forms of the adjective, not two different verbs.

lessons.title: Order and ask politely
lessons.body: Molim and hvala help make a request polite. Želim means I would like or I want. In Vodu, molim, voda changes to vodu; nouns can change form according to their role in a sentence.

lessons.title: Ask and say no
lessons.body: Ne usually comes before a verb: razumijem means I understand, while ne razumijem means I do not understand. A polite question can use Govorite li...? Another common pattern is Da li govorite...?

lessons.title: Find a place and make a plan
lessons.body: Gdje or gde asks where. Danas means today; sutra and sjutra mean tomorrow. Some small words change the noun form: u gradu means in the city, while u grad can express movement into the city.

placement.prompt: Which greeting is appropriate during the day?
placement.feedback: Dobar dan is a daytime greeting. Laku noć means good night; hvala means thank you.

placement.prompt: Which phrase asks a stranger politely how they are?
placement.feedback: Kako ste? is polite singular or plural. Kako si? is familiar singular.

placement.prompt: What does Zovem se Ana mean?
placement.feedback: Zovem se introduces the speaker's name.

placement.prompt: Which Latin form matches the Cyrillic добар дан?
placement.feedback: Добар дан and dobar dan are the same words in two scripts.
Mlijeko is an Ijekavian form; mleko is an Ekavian form. Voda is water and čaj is tea.

placement.prompt: You want to order water. Which phrase fits?

options.text: I do not know your name.

placement.feedback: Ne makes the verb negative. Ne razumem is an Ekavian alternative.

placement.prompt: A woman says she is hungry. Which example fits?
placement.feedback: Gladna is the feminine form here; gladan is masculine.

placement.prompt: Which question asks where the hotel is?
placement.feedback: Gdje je hotel? asks where the hotel is. Gde je hotel? is another valid form.

placement.prompt: Read: Danas sam kod kuće. Sutra idem u grad. When am I going to town?
placement.feedback: Sutra means tomorrow; sjutra is also used in Montenegro.

placement.prompt: Which pair means the same thing in Ijekavian and Ekavian?
placement.feedback: Gdje and gde both mean where. Danas and sutra mean today and tomorrow.

placement.prompt: Which phrase politely asks someone to repeat?
placement.feedback: Možete li ponoviti? means Could you repeat?

placement.prompt: Write ‘thank you’ in the language. Either script is welcome.
placement.feedback: Hvala / хвала means thank you. Other longer expressions of thanks may also be correct; these are the model answers.

placement.prompt: Write ‘I do not understand’. Use either an Ekavian or Ijekavian form, in either script.
placement.feedback: Ne razumijem and ne razumem are two forms. Accept equivalent punctuation and capitalization; other valid wording may exist.

placement.prompt: Write ‘Where is the hotel?’ using either gdje or gde, in either script.
placement.feedback: Gdje je hotel? and Gde je hotel? are both valid. Equivalent punctuation and capitalization should be accepted.

placement.prompt: Read: A: Imate li čaj? B: Da, imamo čaj i kafu. What does B say?
placement.feedback: Da means yes; imamo čaj i kafu means we have tea and coffee.

placement_guidance: These questions sample basic reading and language recognition only. They do not measure listening, speaking or writing independently, cannot establish a CEFR level, and are not a substitute for an institutional assessment. For text questions, ignore case and punctuation, preserve meaningful diacritics and recognize the listed scripts. If an unlisted answer may be valid, show the model answers and offer self-assessment instead of declaring the learner wrong.

dialogues.title: Meeting a person
dialogues.context: Two people meet for the first time.

lines.speaker: A
lines.english: Good day! My name is Ana.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Dobar dan, Ana. Ja sam Marko. Drago mi je.
lines.english: Good day, Ana. I am Marko. Pleased to meet you.

dialogues.practice_prompt: Introduce yourself, then greet someone politely.

dialogues.title: At a cafe

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Dobar dan. Vodu i čaj, molim.
lines.english: Good day. Water and tea, please.

dialogues.practice_prompt: Ask for water or tea, and thank the person serving you.

dialogues.title: Finding a hotel

lines.speaker: A
lines.english: Excuse me, where is the hotel?

dialogues.variant_notes: Gde is an Ekavian alternative to gdje. Oprostite is another polite way to say excuse me, including common Croatian usage.
dialogues.practice_prompt: Ask where the hotel is using either gdje or gde.

dialogues.title: Ask someone to repeat
dialogues.context: A learner needs a little help.

lines.speaker: A
lines.english: Excuse me, I do not understand.

dialogues.variant_notes: Ne razumem is an Ekavian alternative.
dialogues.practice_prompt: Say you do not understand and politely ask for repetition.

dialogues.title: Make a plan

lines.speaker: A
lines.english: Shall we see each other tomorrow?

dialogues.variant_notes: Sjutra is another form heard in Montenegro; Croatian also commonly uses obitelj for family.
dialogues.practice_prompt: Arrange to meet tomorrow and greet a friend's family.

rhythm.title: A small greeting chant
english: Thank you very much, thank you,
See you; have a pleasant day!
rhythm.usage_note: Read or speak to a steady beat. This original text is not a recording or a traditional song; pronunciation and rhythm need native review.
